title: Hello, Family!
subtitle: Greetings, introducing yourself, and asking people to repeat
goal: Greet everyone at the right time of day, answer 'How are you?' and 'Where are you from?', and - most important - stop a conversation politely when you don't understand.

chunks.speaker: Nanay
chunks.tip: Maayong = good (as a greeting). Buntag = morning. Use it until about 11 a.m.
chunks.check: Is it natural for Nanay to greet him by first name like this?

chunks.en: Good morning to you too, Mom.
chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: pud = too / also. Nay is short for Nanay (Mom). Many families also say Ma.
chunks.check: In Bohol, which is most natural: pud, pod, or sad?

chunks.speaker: Tatay
chunks.tip: Hapon = afternoon (about 1 p.m. until dark). Around noon people say Maayong udto.

chunks.speaker: Inday
chunks.tip: Gabii = evening / night. Used as a hello after dark. For bedtime, many families just say 'Good night' in English.
chunks.check: At bedtime, do families say 'Maayong gabii' or the English 'Good night'?

chunks.speaker: Nanay
chunks.tip: Kumusta comes from Spanish 'como esta'. ka = you.

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: ko = I. man is a small softening word - it makes you sound relaxed and friendly. Ikaw = you (when it stands alone).
chunks.check: Or is 'Maayo ra man ko' more common as a reply?

chunks.speaker: Nanay
chunks.tip: ra = just. 'Maayo ra' = just fine, doing okay.

chunks.en: (Asking for the blessing) Your hand, Mom.
chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: Say this as you take an elder's right hand and touch the back of it to your forehead. See today's culture note.
chunks.check: In Bohol, do people say 'Mano, Nay' or 'Mano po, Nay' (with Tagalog 'po')? Or just reach for the hand silently?

chunks.speaker: Nanay
chunks.lit: May the Lord have mercy on you
chunks.tip: What elders say after you do the mano. Often shortened to 'Kaloy-an ka.'

chunks.speaker: Tatay
chunks.tip: pag-abot = arrival. sa = in / at / to.
chunks.check: Would Tatay say this, or just 'Welcome!' in English?

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: si goes before a person's name. You'll hear it everywhere: si Jiana, si Nanay.

chunks.speaker: Kuya
chunks.tip: taga- = from (a place). asa = where.

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: Swap in your state or city: Taga-Texas ko. Taga-Chicago ko.
chunks.check: Most natural spelling/word: Taga-America, Taga-Amerika, or Taga-States?

chunks.speaker: Dodong
chunks.tip: kabalo = know how to. In Bohol people call their language Bisaya (Binisaya) rather than 'Cebuano'.
chunks.check: kabalo vs kahibalo - which does a Bohol family use more?

chunks.en: Just a little. I'm still learning.
chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: gamay ra = just a little. pa = still. Nagtuon = studying / learning.
chunks.check: Is 'Nagtuon pa ko' natural here, or 'Nagkat-on pa ko'?

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: Your number-one survival word. Say it with a rising, friendly tone. 'Unsa man?' sounds even softer.
chunks.check: Is plain 'Unsa?' polite enough toward his girlfriend's parents, or should he say 'Unsa man, Nay?'

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: hinay = slow. Doubled, it means nice and slow. palihug = please.

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: wala = didn't / not. kasabot = understand. In fast speech you'll hear 'Wa ko kasabot.'

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: From balik = again / return.
chunks.check: Balika vs Usba - which is more natural for 'say it again'?

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: ana = that (what was just said). Families mix English into Bisaya all the time, so this question is completely natural.

chunks.speaker: Jiana
chunks.tip: Same root as kasabot. Expect to hear this one a lot.

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: Oo = yes. Note: nakasabot ko (I understood) but wala ko kasabot (I didn't understand).

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: Sige = okay / sure / go ahead. One of the most useful words in Bisaya.

chunks.speaker: Thomas
chunks.tip: kaayo = very.

chunks.speaker: Nanay
chunks.tip: Many people also just say 'Welcome!' in English.
chunks.check: Is 'Walay sapayan' still common, or do most families say 'Welcome' / 'Way problema'?

lines.speaker: Jiana
lines.ceb: Maayong buntag diri, Thomas! Maayong gabii diha!
lines.en: Good morning here, Thomas! Good evening there!
lines.check: diri / diha (here / there) natural in this joke about the time difference?

lines.speaker: Thomas
lines.en: Good evening, Jiana! How are you?

lines.speaker: Jiana
lines.ceb: Maayo ra man. Unsa'y imong gibuhat karon?
lines.en: I'm fine. What are you doing now?
lines.check: Should be spoken at normal, fast-ish speed.

lines.speaker: Jiana
lines.check: Same sentence, said slowly with pauses.

lines.speaker: Thomas
lines.ceb: Wala ko kasabot. Unsa'y English ana?
lines.en: I don't understand. What's that in English?

lines.speaker: Jiana
lines.ceb: 'What are you doing now?' Nakasabot ka?
lines.en: 'What are you doing now?' Did you understand?

lines.speaker: Thomas
lines.en: Yes, I understood. Thank you very much!

lines.speaker: Jiana
lines.ceb: Okay ra. Hinay-hinay lang ta, ha?
lines.en: It's okay. We'll take it slow, okay?
lines.check: Is 'Hinay-hinay lang ta, ha?' natural for 'we'll take it slow'?

lines.speaker: Thomas
lines.en: Good afternoon to you too, Inday.
lines.check: Is it natural for him to call Jiana's younger sister 'Inday'?

days.title: Greetings for every time of day
days.intro: Bisaya greetings follow the clock. Learn the three you'll hear every single day.

culture.title: Greetings follow the clock - and the Bohol accent
culture.text: Maayong buntag (morning, until about 11), Maayong udto (around noon), Maayong hapon (afternoon), Maayong gabii (evening). In Bohol you may hear the y sound turn into j: 'Maajong buntag' instead of 'Maayong buntag'. It's the same word - just the local accent. Jiana's family may tease you kindly if you copy it.

days.title: How are you? Thank you!
days.intro: The first question Nanay will ask you, plus the two words that will get you through every meal.

culture.title: Little words, big friendliness
culture.text: Bisaya is full of tiny words like man, ra and pud. They don't translate neatly, but they make speech sound warm instead of blunt. Don't analyze them - just learn them inside the phrases, exactly as written.

exercises.context: Nanay puts a plate of food in front of you.

days.title: Respect: the Mano
days.intro: One gesture and three words that will win over Nanay and Tatay the moment you walk in.

culture.title: The Mano (blessing)
culture.text: When you greet an older relative, take their right hand, bow slightly, and gently touch the back of their hand to your forehead while saying 'Mano, Nay' or 'Mano, Tay'. They answer 'Kaloy-an ka sa Ginoo' (God bless you). Jiana's parents may be close to your own age, so ask Jiana first whether they'd like you to do it - but most families are deeply touched when a foreign partner makes the effort. Grandparents (Lolo, Lola) should always get a mano.

exercises.context: You walk into the house and see Nanay. You want to show respect.

days.title: Who are you? Where are you from?
days.intro: Every relative and neighbor will ask you the same few questions. Here are the questions - and your answers.

culture.title: Bisaya, Cebuano, Boholano
culture.text: Linguists call the language Cebuano. People in Bohol usually call it Bisaya or Binisaya, and some proudly call their version Boholano. If you say 'Nagtuon ko og Bisaya' (I'm studying Bisaya), expect big smiles - and a lot of relatives testing you.

exercises.context: A cousin you've never met smiles and shakes your hand.

days.title: Survival: Stop! Slow down! Again!
days.intro: The most important phrases of the whole course. With these, no conversation can leave you completely lost.

culture.title: Don't just smile and nod
culture.text: Asking someone to repeat is not rude - it shows you're really trying. The trap is nodding along when you're lost; the family will think you understood. Another trap: people kindly switch to English to help you. If you want to practice, smile and say 'Bisaya lang, hinay-hinay lang.' (Just Bisaya, slowly.)

exercises.context: Nanay says something fast. You didn't catch a single word.
Inday repeated it slowly, but you still have no idea what it means.
You almost caught it. You want to hear it one more time.

days.title: Checking understanding (Bisaya + English)
days.intro: Ask for the English, say whether you understood, and agree with one magic word.

culture.title: Bisaya + English is normal
culture.text: Filipino families switch between Bisaya and English constantly, often in the same sentence: 'Okay ra, hinay-hinay lang ta.' You are not 'cheating' when you mix in English - you're talking the way they do. Asking 'Unsa'y English ana?' is something even locals say.

exercises.context: Jiana says, 'Let's eat later, okay?' You agree.
Jiana uses a Bisaya word you don't know. You want the English.

days.title: Putting it together
days.intro: No new phrases today. Listen to three real-life conversations, answer as Thomas, then do your video-call mission.

culture.title: Video calls and the time difference
culture.text: The Philippines is 12 to 16 hours ahead of the U.S. mainland (it never changes for daylight saving). So your evening is usually Jiana's morning. Greet her with her time of day, not yours - she'll notice.

mission.title: Video-call mission: Week 1
steps: Greet Jiana with HER time of day (Maayong buntag / hapon / gabii).
Ask 'Kumusta ka?' and answer when she asks you back.
Ask her to say one sentence in fast Bisaya. Answer with 'Unsa? Hinay-hinay lang, palihug.'
When she repeats it, say 'Wala ko kasabot. Unsa'y English ana?'
If Nanay or Inday walks by on camera, greet them too: 'Maayong buntag, Nay!'
End with 'Sige, salamat!' and ask Jiana how your pronunciation was.

reviewExtras.check: Is this description of the Bohol accent accurate and not offensive?

reviewExtras.en: (Asking for the blessing) Your hand, Dad.

reviewExtras.check: Natural way to ask people not to switch to English?

reviewExtras.en: It's okay, let's take it slow.
